content.text: The text reviews membranous enteritis, dysentery, typhlitis, intestinal ulcers, hemorrhage, obstruction, and intestinal cancer. It describes their pathology, symptoms, differential diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, and largely historical treatments. Dysentery involves inflammatory injury of the large intestine, producing tenesmus and mucus-, pus-, blood-, and tissue-containing stools; sanitation, safe water, irrigation, ipecacuanha, rest, and nutrition are emphasized. Typhlitis centers on the caecum or appendix and may cause abscess, perforation, or peritonitis. Ulcers may arise from infection, toxins, trauma, tuberculosis, or impaired circulation, with bleeding and perforation as major dangers. Obstruction may be acute or chronic, caused by impaction, volvulus, strangulation, intussusception, strictures, tumors, or adhesions; opium, cautious enemas, and timely surgery are discussed. Cancer causes progressive obstruction, wasting, and palpable tumors. Mary travelled to the hallway. Daniel journeyed to the bedroom. John went back to the garden.
